title: 10  Inference
text: 10.1 Learning Objectives

title: 10  Inference
text:
Understand the distinction between identification and statistical inference
Recognize when classical standard errors are invalid
Apply robust and clustered standard errors in applied settings
Interpret statistical significance in IV and DiD designs

title: 10  Inference
text:
10.2 Key Takeaways

Identification answers what is estimated; inference answers how precisely
Classical standard errors rely on strong assumptions rarely satisfied in practice
Robust and clustered standard errors are essential in applied econometrics
Incorrect inference can overturn otherwise credible identification strategies

title: 10  Inference
text:
10.3 Common Pitfalls

Confusing statistical significance with causal validity
Using heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors when clustering is required
Clustering at the wrong level
Ignoring serial correlation in panel and DiD settings

title: 10  Inference
text:
10.4 Why Inference Matters
Identification establishes causal interpretation under assumptions. Inference quantifies uncertainty around estimated effects. A well-identified estimate with invalid inference can lead to misleading conclusions.

title: 10  Inference
text:
10.5 Classical Standard Errors
Classical standard errors assume: - homoskedasticity - no serial correlation - independent observations
These assumptions rarely hold in observational data.

title: 10  Inference
text:
10.6 Heteroskedasticity-Robust Standard Errors
Robust standard errors allow for: - unknown heteroskedasticity - consistent variance estimation under weaker assumptions
They are standard in cross-sectional applications but insufficient in panel settings.

title: 10  Inference
text:
10.7 Clustered Standard Errors
Clustering accounts for: - within-group correlation - serial dependence over time
Correct clustering is dictated by the level of treatment variation. Difference-in-Differences and panel regressions typically require clustering at the unit level.

title: 10  Inference
text:
10.8 Inference in IV and DiD
Instrumental Variables: - weak instruments inflate variance - standard errors reflect identification strength
Difference-in-Differences: - serial correlation leads to over-rejection - clustering is essential for valid inference

title: 10  Inference
text:
10.9 Practical Guidance

Cross-section: use heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors
Panel data: cluster at the individual or group level
DiD: cluster at the treatment assignment level
Small number of clusters requires caution in interpretation

title: 12  Real Data Case 2: Government Consumption and Economic Growth
text:
12.1 Introduction
Government spending plays a central role in macroeconomic policy. While higher public consumption may stabilize the business cycle and provide essential public services, it may also crowd out private investment and reduce long-run economic growth. This case study examines the empirical relationship between government consumption and economic growth using a macroeconomic panel dataset covering a large number of countries over several decades. The goal is to demonstrate the use of fixed effects panel regression to control for unobserved heterogeneity across countries and common global shocks over time.

title: 12  Real Data Case 2: Government Consumption and Economic Growth
text:
12.9 Results
Quantitatively, the point estimate implies that a one‑percentage‑point increase in government consumption (as a share of GDP) is associated with approximately a 0.12 percentage point lower GDP per capita growth rate within a country. The estimate is not statistically significant at conventional levels, so the magnitude should be interpreted cautiously.
The estimated coefficient on government consumption captures the within-country association between changes in government consumption and changes in economic growth, net of global time effects. A negative coefficient suggests that increases in government consumption are associated with lower growth rates within countries over time, although statistical significance must be carefully evaluated. Clustering standard errors at the country level accounts for serial correlation and heteroskedasticity within countries.
crumbs: 12  Real Data Case 2: Government Consumption and Economic Growth

title: 12  Real Data Case 2: Government Consumption and Economic Growth
text:
12.10 Interpretation and Caveats
It is important to emphasize that this analysis identifies correlation, not causation. Potential concerns include:

reverse causality (growth downturns may raise government spending)
omitted time-varying country-specific factors
measurement error in macroeconomic aggregates

Nevertheless, the fixed effects framework provides a useful baseline for understanding empirical patterns in cross-country panel data.
crumbs: 12  Real Data Case 2: Government Consumption and Economic Growth

title: 12  Real Data Case 2: Government Consumption and Economic Growth
text:
12.11 Concluding Remarks
This case study illustrates how fixed effects panel models can be used to study macroeconomic relationships using multi-country data.
By controlling for country and year fixed effects, the analysis isolates within-country variation and highlights how accounting for unobserved heterogeneity can substantially alter naive cross-sectional relationships. While the results do not support a statistically significant association between government consumption and economic growth, the exercise demonstrates a clean and reproducible workflow for applied macroeconometric analysis using real-world data.
crumbs: 12  Real Data Case 2: Government Consumption and Economic Growth

title: 13  Micro Case 3A: Simulated Job Training Program
text:
13.7 Difference in Means
The simplest estimator of the treatment effect compares mean outcomes between treated and untreated individuals.
Formally, the difference-in-means estimator is:
\[
E[y \mid D = 1] - E[y \mid D = 0]
\]
This estimator does not control for selection into treatment and may therefore be biased if treatment status is correlated with unobserved ability.


Code
mean_treated   <- mean(case3A$y[case3A$treat == 1])
mean_untreated <- mean(case3A$y[case3A$treat == 0])

diff_means <- mean_treated - mean_untreated

c(
  mean_treated   = mean_treated,
  mean_untreated = mean_untreated,
  diff_in_means  = diff_means
)


  mean_treated mean_untreated  diff_in_means 
     12.922176       9.191867       3.730309 


The estimated difference in means captures both the causal effect of the program and any pre-existing differences between treated and untreated individuals.

13.10 True ATE vs Estimated Effects
Because the data are simulated, we observe potential outcomes for each individual. This allows us to compute the true average treatment effect (ATE) directly.
The true ATE is defined as:
\[

\]


Code

true_ate

13.11 Instrumental Variables
In many empirical applications, relevant control variables such as ability are unobserved. In such cases, ordinary least squares estimation remains biased.
An alternative identification strategy relies on instrumental variables. An instrument affects treatment participation but has no direct effect on the outcome.
In this simulation, the variable \(z\) serves as an instrument for program participation.

13.11.1 First Stage
The first-stage regression relates treatment participation to the instrument:
\[
D_i = \pi_0 + \pi_1 z_i + v_i

14.1 Introduction
This micro case illustrates the consequences of using weak instruments in instrumental variables estimation.

title: 17  Difference-in-Differences: Intuition
text:
17.1 Motivation
Difference-in-differences (DiD) is a causal inference method used when treatment is assigned at a group level and varies over time.
The key idea is simple:
we compare changes over time, not levels.

title: 17  Difference-in-Differences: Intuition
text:
17.2 Basic Setup
Consider two groups: - a treated group - a control group
And two time periods: - before treatment - after treatment
The DiD estimator compares the change in outcomes for the treated group to the change in outcomes for the control group.

title: 17  Difference-in-Differences: Intuition
text:
17.3 Parallel Trends Assumption





Parallel trends assumption: treated and control groups evolve similarly before treatment

title: 18  Difference-in-Differences: Canonical 2×2
text:
18.1 Setup
We consider the canonical difference-in-differences setup with: - two groups (treated and control) - two time periods (before and after treatment)
Treatment affects only the treated group in the post-treatment period.

title: 18  Difference-in-Differences: Canonical 2×2
text:
18.2 The DiD Estimator
The DiD estimator is defined as:
\[
\text{DiD} = (\bar Y_{T,post} - \bar Y_{T,pre}) - (\bar Y_{C,post} - \bar Y_{C,pre})
\]

title: 18  Difference-in-Differences: Canonical 2×2
text:
18.5 Inference in Difference-in-Differences
In the canonical 2×2 design, the DiD regression is fully saturated. As a result, the treatment effect is exactly identified, but standard errors are not defined.
This illustrates an important point: in the 2×2 case, difference-in-differences is an algebraic identity rather than a statistical model.
Meaningful inference requires additional units or time periods, which we consider in later sections.

title: 18  Difference-in-Differences: Canonical 2×2
text:
18.6 Parallel Trends Assumption
The key identifying assumption underlying difference-in-differences is the parallel trends assumption.
In the absence of treatment, the average outcomes of the treated and control groups would have followed the same time trend.
Formally, the assumption requires:
\[
E[Y_{0t}^T - Y_{0,t-1}^T] = E[Y_{0t}^C - Y_{0,t-1}^C]
\]
where \(Y_{0t}\) denotes the potential outcome without treatment.
This assumption is fundamentally untestable, but its plausibility can be assessed using pre-treatment data.

title: 19  Difference-in-Differences: Event Study
text:
19.1 Motivation
While the parallel trends assumption is fundamentally untestable, event-study designs allow researchers to assess its plausibility by examining pre-treatment dynamics.
An event study extends the difference-in-differences framework by estimating dynamic treatment effects relative to the timing of the intervention.

title: 19  Difference-in-Differences: Event Study
text:
19.2 Event Study Specification
Let \(k\) index time relative to treatment, with \(k = 0\) denoting the treatment period.
The event-study regression can be written as:
\[
Y_{it} = \alpha + \sum_{k \neq -1} \delta_k \mathbf{1}(t - T_i = k) + \mu_i + \lambda_t + u_{it}
\]
where \(k = -1\) is the omitted baseline period.
Under parallel trends, the coefficients \(\delta_k\) for \(k < 0\) should be close to zero.

21.4 Why TWFE Can Be Misleading
With staggered adoption, treated units serve as controls for later-treated units. As a result, the TWFE estimator implicitly compares already-treated units to newly treated units.
This can induce negative or inappropriate weights, even when treatment effects are homogeneous.

title: 21  Difference-in-Differences: Staggered Adoption and TWFE Bias
text:
21.5 Intuition: Forbidden Comparisons
Comparisons between treated and not-yet-treated units are valid. Comparisons where treated units act as controls for other treated units are not.
TWFE does not distinguish between these comparisons.

title: 21  Difference-in-Differences: Staggered Adoption and TWFE Bias
text:
21.6 Implications
Event-study plots based on TWFE may also be misleading in staggered settings.

title: 21  Difference-in-Differences: Staggered Adoption and TWFE Bias

21.7 Looking Ahead
The limitations of the two-way fixed effects estimator in staggered adoption settings raise an important question: how should difference-in-differences be implemented when treatment timing varies across units?
Recent methodological advances propose alternative estimators that explicitly account for treatment timing and avoid the forbidden comparisons implicit in TWFE.
The next chapter introduces these modern difference-in-differences estimators and shows how they resolve the problems highlighted here.

title: 23  Difference-in-Differences: Summary and Decision Tree
text:
23.1 Purpose of This Chapter
This chapter summarizes the core lessons from the Difference-in-Differences (DiD) block and provides a practical decision tree for choosing an appropriate DiD estimator in applied work.
Rather than introducing new estimators, the goal is to help researchers map their empirical design to the correct identification strategy and avoid common pitfalls, especially in settings with multiple time periods and staggered treatment adoption.

title: 23  Difference-in-Differences: Summary and Decision Tree
text:
23.2 What Difference-in-Differences Identifies
Difference-in-Differences does not identify a generic treatment effect. Instead, it identifies average causal effects under specific comparison structures.
At its core, DiD relies on comparing changes over time between treated units and an appropriate control group.
The key identifying assumption is a version of the parallel trends assumption: in the absence of treatment, treated and control units would have followed the same outcome evolution.
Who is used as a control group and when the comparison is made determines which causal parameter is identified.

title: 23  Difference-in-Differences: Summary and Decision Tree
text:
23.3 Key Design Dimensions in DiD
Before choosing an estimator, an applied researcher should answer four design questions.

23.3.1 Number of Time Periods

Two periods only
More than two periods



23.3.2 Treatment Timing

All treated units receive treatment at the same time
Treatment adoption is staggered across units



23.3.3 Treatment Effect Heterogeneity

Constant treatment effects
Effects vary across cohorts or over time



23.3.4 Anticipation and Dynamics

No anticipation
Possible anticipation effects
Dynamic treatment effects

These features determine whether standard two-way fixed effects estimators are valid.

title: 23  Difference-in-Differences: Summary and Decision Tree
text:
23.4 The DiD Decision Tree

23.4.1 Step 1: Is the design 2×2?
One treated group, one control group, one pre-treatment period, and one post-treatment period.
Yes → Canonical DiD or TWFE is appropriate.
No → Proceed to Step 2.



23.4.2 Step 2: Are there multiple time periods with staggered treatment adoption?
Yes → Standard TWFE is generally invalid due to forbidden comparisons. Proceed to Step 3.
No → TWFE may still be valid under strong homogeneity assumptions.



23.4.3 Step 3: Do treatment effects vary across cohorts or over time?
Yes → Use modern DiD estimators: - Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021) - Sun and Abraham (2021)
No → TWFE may approximate an average effect, but caution is required.



23.4.4 Step 4: Is an event-study interpretation desired?
Yes → Use interaction-weighted event-study estimators (Sun and Abraham).
No → Use aggregated group-time effects (Callaway and Sant’Anna).

title: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference
text:
24.1 Purpose of This Chapter
This chapter provides a unified empirical design checklist that synthesizes the methods covered throughout this book.
Rather than focusing on a specific estimator, the goal is to offer a systematic framework for moving from a research question to a credible causal design. The checklist is intended to be used when designing a new project, evaluating existing empirical work, or interpreting applied research results.
crumbs: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference

title: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference
text:
24.2 Research Question and Causal Parameter
Every empirical project begins with a research question, but credible inference requires translating that question into a well-defined causal parameter.
Key questions include:

What is the treatment or intervention?
Who is treated, and relative to whom?
When does treatment occur?
What is the outcome of interest?
What counterfactual outcome is being considered?

Clarity about the estimand is essential before any discussion of data or estimation.
crumbs: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference

title: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference
text:
24.3 Data Structure
The structure of the data constrains the set of feasible identification strategies.
Important considerations include:

Cross-sectional, repeated cross-sectional, or panel data
Level of observation versus level of treatment
Timing and frequency of observations
Presence of untreated or not-yet-treated units

A mismatch between the research question and the data structure is a common source of invalid empirical designs.
crumbs: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference

title: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference
text:
24.4 Identification Strategy
Identification comes from assumptions, not from estimation techniques.
Common identification strategies include:

Selection on observables
Difference-in-Differences
Instrumental Variables
Regression Discontinuity Designs
Synthetic Control and panel-based causal methods

The chosen strategy should be justified by institutional knowledge and the data-generating process.
crumbs: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference

title: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference
text:
24.5 Assumptions: Explicit and Implicit
Each identification strategy relies on assumptions that must be stated clearly.
Examples include:

Parallel trends
Exclusion restrictions
No anticipation
Continuity at a cutoff
Stable Unit Treatment Value Assumption (SUTVA)

Empirical credibility depends on whether these assumptions are plausible in the context under study.
crumbs: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference

title: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference
text:
24.6 Threats to Identification
Even well-designed studies face potential threats to identification.
Common threats include:

Time-varying confounders
Changes in sample composition
Spillovers and general equilibrium effects
Endogenous policy timing
Functional form dependence

Identifying and discussing these threats is a central component of applied work.
crumbs: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference

title: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference
text:
24.7 Estimation Choices
Once identification is established, estimation choices should follow logically.
Researchers should be explicit about:

Why a particular estimator is used
Which comparisons drive identification
How units and time periods are weighted
Sensitivity to alternative specifications

Estimation should support identification, not replace it.
crumbs: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference

title: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference
text:
24.8 Inference
Valid inference requires aligning standard errors with the source of identifying variation.
Key issues include:

Appropriate clustering level
Number of clusters
Serial correlation
Finite-sample concerns

Inference choices should be justified with reference to the empirical design.
crumbs: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference

title: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference
text:
24.9 Diagnostics and Falsification
Credible empirical work includes diagnostics that probe the identifying assumptions.
Common tools include:

Placebo tests
Event-study analyses
Balance and pre-trend tests
Sensitivity and robustness checks

These exercises strengthen the interpretation of causal estimates.
crumbs: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference

title: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference
text:
24.10 Interpretation and External Validity
Empirical results should be interpreted in light of the design.
Important questions include:

To whom does the estimated effect apply?
Which margins of variation identify the effect?
How policy-relevant is the estimate?
What limits external validity?

Clear interpretation prevents overgeneralization.
crumbs: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference

title: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference
text:
24.11 A One-Page Empirical Design Checklist
Before finalizing an empirical analysis, a researcher should be able to answer the following questions:

What is the causal question and estimand?
What is the source of identifying variation?
Which assumptions are required?
What threatens identification?
Why is the chosen estimator appropriate?
How is inference conducted?
How should the results be interpreted?

If any of these questions cannot be answered clearly, the empirical design should be reconsidered.
crumbs: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference

title: 24  Empirical Design Checklist: From Research Question to Credible Causal Inference
text:
24.12 Concluding Remarks
Applied econometrics is fundamentally about design.
Careful attention to identification, assumptions, and interpretation is more important than the choice of estimator. This checklist provides a general framework for disciplined empirical work and serves as a bridge to more advanced causal methods beyond Difference-in-Differences.

title: 25  Regression Discontinuity Designs
text:
25.1 Purpose and Intuition of RDD
Regression discontinuity designs (RDD) exploit situations in which treatment assignment is determined by whether an observed running variable crosses a known cutoff. Units just above and just below the cutoff are assumed to be comparable in all respects except for treatment status.
The core idea of RDD is that, in a sufficiently small neighborhood around the cutoff, the assignment mechanism mimics randomization. While treatment is not randomly assigned in the population at large, it is as good as random for units whose value of the running variable lies arbitrarily close to the threshold.
As a result, discontinuities in the conditional expectation of the outcome at the cutoff can be interpreted as causal treatment effects.
Formally, let \(X_i\) denote the running variable and let \(c\) denote the cutoff. Treatment assignment depends on whether the running variable crosses this threshold. The estimand of interest is the discontinuity in the conditional expectation of the outcome:
\[
\tau = \lim_{x \downarrow c} E[Y_i \mid X_i = x]
      - \lim_{x \uparrow c} E[Y_i \mid X_i = x].
\]
This estimand captures a local average treatment effect at the cutoff rather than a population-wide effect. The local nature of identification is a defining feature of RDD and has important implications for interpretation and external validity.
RDD is particularly attractive in applied work because the source of identification is transparent. Unlike regression adjustment, which relies on functional form assumptions, or difference-in-differences designs, which require parallel trends, RDD relies on a single and conceptually clear condition: in the absence of treatment, the outcome would evolve smoothly through the cutoff.

title: 25  Regression Discontinuity Designs
section: 25.2 Sharp and Fuzzy Regression Discontinuity Designs
text:
25.2 Sharp and Fuzzy Regression Discontinuity Designs
Regression discontinuity designs come in two closely related variants, depending on how treatment assignment responds to crossing the cutoff: sharp RDD and fuzzy RDD. The distinction is crucial for both identification and estimation.

25.2.1 Sharp Regression Discontinuity
\[
D_i = \mathbf{1}\{X_i \ge c\}.
\]
In a sharp RDD, the probability of treatment jumps from zero to one at the cutoff. Under continuity of potential outcomes, the causal effect at the threshold is given by the discontinuity in the outcome regression:
\[
\tau = \lim_{x \downarrow c} E[Y_i \mid X_i = x]
      - \lim_{x \uparrow c} E[Y_i \mid X_i = x].
\]
This estimand captures a local treatment effect at the cutoff.


25.2.2 Fuzzy Regression Discontinuity
In many applications, crossing the cutoff affects the probability of treatment without perfectly determining it.
\[
\tau = \frac{
\lim_{x \downarrow c} E[Y_i \mid X_i = x]
- \lim_{x \uparrow c} E[Y_i \mid X_i = x]
}{
\lim_{x \downarrow c} E[D_i \mid X_i = x]
- \lim_{x \uparrow c} E[D_i \mid X_i = x]
}.
\]
This estimand identifies a local average treatment effect for compliers at the cutoff. NA

title: 25  Regression Discontinuity Designs
text:
25.3 Graphical Analysis
Graphical analysis is a central component of any regression discontinuity design. Before conducting formal estimation, researchers should visually inspect the relationship between the outcome variable and the running variable around the cutoff.
The purpose of RD plots is not to estimate treatment effects precisely, but to assess the plausibility of the identifying assumptions and to make the source of identification transparent.
In a credible RDD, the conditional expectation of the outcome should evolve smoothly with the running variable on either side of the cutoff, while exhibiting a visible discontinuity at the threshold.

title: 25  Regression Discontinuity Designs
text:
25.4 Estimation and Bandwidth Choice
While graphical analysis provides intuition and a valuable credibility check, causal inference in regression discontinuity designs requires formal estimation. The key challenge is to estimate the discontinuity in the conditional expectation of the outcome at the cutoff while balancing bias and variance.
RDD estimation is inherently local. Observations far from the cutoff may improve precision but risk introducing bias due to misspecification of the functional form. Observations very close to the cutoff are more comparable but yield noisier estimates. The choice of bandwidth reflects this fundamental trade-off.

25.4.1 Local Polynomial Estimation
The standard approach to RDD estimation is local polynomial regression, estimated separately on each side of the cutoff. In practice, local linear regression is often preferred due to its favorable boundary properties.
Let (Y_i) denote the outcome and (X_i) the running variable with cutoff (c). A local linear RDD estimator solves:
\[
\min_{\alpha_\ell,\beta_\ell}
\sum_{i: X_i < c}
K\!\left(\frac{X_i - c}{h}\right)
\left(Y_i - \alpha_\ell - \beta_\ell (X_i - c)\right)^2
\]
and analogously on the right side of the cutoff. The estimated treatment effect is given by the difference in the fitted intercepts at the cutoff.


25.4.2 Bandwidth Choice: Bias–Variance Trade-off
The bandwidth (h) determines how local the comparison is.

Small bandwidths reduce bias but increase variance.
Large bandwidths reduce variance but risk bias from functional form misspecification.

Graphical analysis helps guide reasonable bandwidth ranges, but formal methods are needed for principled selection.


25.4.3 Data-Driven Bandwidth Selection
Modern RDD practice relies on data-driven bandwidth selectors that minimize asymptotic mean squared error. Among the most widely used are the methods proposed by Imbens and Kalyanaraman (2012) and Calonico, Cattaneo, and Titiunik (2014).
These procedures automatically choose bandwidths that balance bias and variance and are implemented in standard software packages.


25.4.4 Reporting and Transparency
Good practice in RDD estimation includes reporting the chosen bandwidth and the method used to select it, presenting robustness checks across bandwidths, pairing numerical estimates with graphical evidence, and clearly stating the local nature of the estimand.
RDD estimates are local by construction. Their credibility rests not on complexity, but on transparency.

title: 25  Regression Discontinuity Designs
text:
25.5 Validity Checks and Manipulation Tests
The credibility of a regression discontinuity design hinges on the plausibility of its identifying assumptions. While RDDs are often viewed as transparent and intuitive, they require careful diagnostic checks to rule out alternative explanations for observed discontinuities.
The key identifying assumption is that, in the absence of treatment, the conditional expectation of the outcome and other relevant variables would evolve smoothly through the cutoff. Validity checks in RDD aim to assess whether this assumption is likely to hold in the data.

25.5.1 Manipulation of the Running Variable
A primary threat to validity arises if individuals can precisely manipulate the running variable in order to sort around the cutoff. If such manipulation occurs, units just above and just below the threshold may no longer be comparable.
One common diagnostic is to examine the density of the running variable around the cutoff. A discontinuity in the density suggests strategic sorting and undermines the credibility of the design.


25.5.2 Continuity of Covariates
Another important validity check involves testing for discontinuities in predetermined covariates at the cutoff. Since these variables should not be affected by treatment, any systematic jumps may indicate violations of the identifying assumptions.
In a credible RDD, baseline characteristics should evolve smoothly through the threshold, mirroring the continuity required of the outcome in the absence of treatment.


25.5.3 Placebo and Falsification Tests
Placebo tests provide an additional diagnostic by estimating discontinuities at cutoffs where no treatment is assigned. Significant effects at placebo thresholds cast doubt on the interpretation of the main RDD estimate.
Similarly, researchers may test for treatment effects in periods or outcomes that should not be affected by the intervention. Failure to find such effects strengthens the credibility of the design.


25.5.4 Limitations of Validity Checks
While validity checks are informative, they cannot conclusively prove identification. Absence of evidence of manipulation or discontinuities in covariates does not guarantee that the identifying assumptions hold.
For this reason, validity checks should be viewed as complementary evidence, to be interpreted alongside substantive knowledge of the institutional context and the graphical and statistical evidence presented earlier.

title: 25  Regression Discontinuity Designs
text:
25.6 Interpretation and External Validity
Regression discontinuity designs identify causal effects at the cutoff of the running variable. As a result, the estimated treatment effect is inherently local and applies only to units whose value of the running variable lies in a neighborhood around the threshold.
This local nature of identification has important implications for interpretation. RDD estimates should not be interpreted as average treatment effects for the entire population, but rather as effects for individuals who are marginal with respect to treatment assignment.

25.6.1 Local Nature of the Estimand
The RDD estimand captures the causal effect for units at the cutoff. These units may differ systematically from those farther away from the threshold, limiting the external validity of the findings.
In some applications, however, individuals near the cutoff are of particular policy relevance. For example, when eligibility rules are defined by thresholds, policymakers are often interested precisely in the effects for marginal recipients.


25.6.2 External Validity and Generalization
The limited external validity of RDD does not imply that the design is uninformative. Instead, it highlights the importance of careful interpretation and contextual knowledge.
Researchers may strengthen external validity by combining RDD evidence with results from other designs, by estimating effects at multiple cutoffs, or by studying heterogeneous treatment effects across subgroups.


25.6.3 Policy Interpretation
RDD results are often well suited for policy evaluation, as they directly speak to the consequences of marginal changes in eligibility or assignment rules.
However, extrapolating RDD estimates beyond the cutoff requires strong assumptions and should be undertaken with caution. Transparency about what is identified�and what is not�is essential for credible policy analysis.


25.6.4 Summary
Regression discontinuity designs offer a powerful and transparent framework for causal inference when treatment assignment is governed by a known threshold. Their credibility rests on local identification, careful estimation, and thorough validity checks.
When interpreted appropriately, RDDs provide compelling evidence on causal effects at policy-relevant margins, even if their conclusions do not automatically generalize to the broader population.

title: 25  Regression Discontinuity Designs
section: 25.7 Empirical Example: Program Eligibility and Test Score Cutoffs
text:
25.7 Empirical Example: Program Eligibility and Test Score Cutoffs
To illustrate the mechanics and interpretation of regression discontinuity designs, we consider a stylized empirical example in which eligibility for a program is determined by a cutoff in a test score.
Suppose students are eligible for an educational intervention if their standardized test score exceeds a known threshold. Let the test score serve as the running variable, with treatment assignment determined by whether the score crosses the cutoff.
The outcome of interest may be a subsequent academic achievement measure, such as grade point average, test performance in a later period, or educational attainment.

25.7.1 Design and Assignment Mechanism
Eligibility for the program is determined by a known cutoff in the test score. Students with scores at or above the threshold are offered treatment, while those below are not.
Near the cutoff, students just above and just below the threshold are expected to be similar in observed and unobserved characteristics, except for their treatment status. Under the continuity assumption, differences in outcomes at the cutoff can be attributed to the causal effect of program participation.
This setting naturally lends itself to a sharp regression discontinuity design if eligibility perfectly determines participation, or to a fuzzy design if take-up is incomplete.


25.7.2 What the RDD Estimates
The regression discontinuity estimand in this setting captures the causal effect of program eligibility for students whose test scores lie in a neighborhood around the cutoff.
Importantly, this effect applies to marginal students near the threshold and should not be interpreted as the average effect for all program participants. The empirical example therefore reinforces the local nature of identification emphasized earlier in the chapter.


25.7.3 Graphical Evidence (Interactive Preview)
Graphical evidence plays a central role in understanding and communicating regression discontinuity designs. In this empirical example, the primary diagnostic tool is a plot of the outcome variable against the running variable, with special attention paid to observations near the cutoff.
An RD plot visually displays whether the conditional expectation of the outcome evolves smoothly on either side of the threshold while exhibiting a discontinuous jump at the cutoff. Such a pattern is consistent with the identifying assumptions of the design.
In practice, raw scatterplots are often supplemented with binned averages and local polynomial fits estimated separately on each side of the cutoff. These graphical elements help reduce noise and clarify the underlying relationship without imposing strong global functional form assumptions.
For the purposes of this chapter, the graphical analysis is presented conceptually. In the accompanying interactive handout, readers will be able to adjust key elements of the RD plot�such as the bandwidth, bin width, and polynomial order�and observe how the visual evidence responds to these choices.
This interactive exploration reinforces two core insights. First, RDD evidence is inherently local: conclusions are driven by observations near the cutoff. Second, graphical results are sensitive to tuning parameters, underscoring the importance of transparency and robustness in applied work.
The graphical analysis should be interpreted as a complement to formal estimation rather than as a standalone source of inference.


25.7.4 Estimation Results (Empirical Illustration)
We now briefly illustrate how formal estimation complements the graphical evidence in this empirical example. The regression discontinuity estimate is obtained using local polynomial regression with a data-driven bandwidth selection procedure.
Consistent with the graphical patterns, the estimated treatment effect indicates a positive and statistically meaningful discontinuity at the cutoff. The magnitude of the effect is economically relevant for students near the eligibility threshold, reinforcing the interpretation of the design as identifying a local causal effect.
To assess robustness, estimates can be computed using alternative bandwidth choices and polynomial orders. In this example, the qualitative conclusions remain stable across a range of reasonable specifications, although point estimates and standard errors vary, reflecting the inherent bias�variance trade-off discussed earlier.
Importantly, these estimates should be interpreted in light of the design�s identifying assumptions and validity checks. The numerical results do not stand alone; they gain credibility from the alignment between graphical evidence, institutional knowledge, and diagnostic tests.
In the interactive handout, readers will be able to modify estimation choices�such as the bandwidth and kernel�and observe how the estimated discontinuity responds to these changes in real time.


25.7.5 Validity Checks (Empirical Illustration)
To assess the credibility of the regression discontinuity design in this empirical example, several standard validity checks are considered. These diagnostics are designed to evaluate whether the identifying assumptions discussed earlier are plausible in the data.
First, the distribution of the running variable is examined around the cutoff to assess potential manipulation. In a credible design, the density of test scores should evolve smoothly through the threshold, with no visible discontinuity that would suggest strategic sorting.
Second, predetermined covariates�such as prior academic performance or demographic characteristics�are analyzed for discontinuities at the cutoff. The absence of systematic jumps in these variables supports the assumption that students just above and below the threshold are comparable.
Third, placebo tests are conducted by estimating discontinuities at alternative cutoffs where no treatment is assigned. Finding no significant effects at these placebo thresholds strengthens confidence that the observed discontinuity at the true cutoff reflects a causal effect of program eligibility.
Taken together, these checks provide supporting evidence for the validity of the design. While no single diagnostic can conclusively establish identification, the consistency of results across multiple tests enhances the credibility of the empirical findings.
In the interactive handout, these validity checks can be explored dynamically, allowing readers to visualize density plots, covariate continuity, and placebo estimates under different specifications.


25.7.6 Transition to the Next Chapter
Regression discontinuity designs exploit deterministic assignment rules to achieve credible causal identification at policy-relevant thresholds. Their strength lies in transparent assumptions and local comparisons near a cutoff.
The next chapter extends the discussion of quasi-experimental methods to settings in which treatment assignment varies over time rather than across a threshold. While the identifying assumptions differ, the central challenge remains the same: isolating causal effects in observational data using institutional structure and careful design.

title: 26  Event Studies and Dynamic Treatment Effects
text:
26.1 Motivation and Intuition
Difference-in-differences methods are often used to estimate average treatment effects before and after a policy intervention. While such estimates are informative, they implicitly impose strong restrictions on how treatment effects evolve over time.
In many empirical settings, treatment effects are not instantaneous and constant. Instead, they may emerge gradually, grow or fade over time, or even exhibit anticipation effects before the formal implementation of a policy. Event studies provide a flexible framework for examining these dynamic treatment effects.
The central idea of an event study is to align units in time relative to a common event, such as the adoption of a policy or the onset of a treatment. Outcomes are then analyzed as a function of event time, rather than calendar time, allowing researchers to trace the evolution of treatment effects before and after the event.
This dynamic perspective serves two important purposes. First, it enables researchers to assess the plausibility of identifying assumptions by examining pre-treatment trends. Second, it allows for a richer interpretation of treatment effects, distinguishing short-run impacts from longer-run adjustments.
Event studies therefore extend the difference-in-differences framework by replacing a single average effect with a sequence of time-specific effects. This shift from static to dynamic analysis is essential in settings where responses unfold over time and where policy relevance depends on understanding adjustment paths rather than only average impacts.

title: 26  Event Studies and Dynamic Treatment Effects
text:
26.2 Event-Time Framework
Event studies reframe the analysis of treatment effects by indexing time relative to the occurrence of a specific event rather than by calendar time. This transformation allows researchers to compare units at comparable stages before and after treatment, even when the timing of treatment varies across units.
Formally, event time is defined as the difference between the current period and the period in which the event occurs. Negative values correspond to pre-treatment periods, zero denotes the period of treatment onset, and positive values represent post-treatment periods. One period—typically the last pre-treatment period—is omitted as a reference category to normalize the effects.
Each event-time coefficient measures the average difference in outcomes between treated and control units at a given relative time, conditional on the chosen normalization. As a result, the sequence of coefficients traces out the dynamic response of the outcome variable to the treatment.
This framework highlights an important distinction between calendar time and event time. While calendar time captures aggregate shocks affecting all units simultaneously, event time isolates the evolution of outcomes relative to treatment adoption. By separating these dimensions, event studies provide a clearer picture of treatment dynamics.
The event-time framework also makes explicit the assumptions required for identification. In particular, the absence of systematic pre-treatment differences across event times underlies the interpretation of post-treatment coefficients as causal effects. These assumptions are examined in detail in the following sections. ## Identification Assumptions
The credibility of event-study estimates rests on a set of identifying assumptions that extend those underlying standard difference-in-differences designs. While the dynamic framework offers greater flexibility, it also makes these assumptions more explicit and, in some cases, more demanding.
The first key assumption is parallel trends in event time. In the absence of treatment, outcomes for treated and control units are assumed to evolve similarly at each relative time period. This assumption implies that differences observed prior to treatment reflect common trends rather than anticipatory responses or differential dynamics.
Closely related is the no anticipation assumption. Units are assumed not to adjust their behavior in response to knowledge of future treatment before the treatment actually occurs. Violations of this assumption may manifest as systematic deviations in pre-treatment event-time coefficients and complicate the interpretation of post-treatment effects.
Event studies make these assumptions empirically assessable. By estimating coefficients for multiple pre-treatment periods, researchers can visually and statistically examine whether outcomes diverge prior to treatment. Flat or statistically insignificant pre-treatment coefficients are often interpreted as supporting evidence for the identifying assumptions.
However, it is important to emphasize that the absence of pre-trends does not guarantee identification. Event-study estimates may still be biased if treatment timing is correlated with unobserved shocks or if treatment effects are heterogeneous over time. These concerns are especially relevant in settings with staggered adoption, where standard two-way fixed effects estimators may produce misleading dynamic patterns.
Taken together, identification in event studies relies on careful institutional reasoning, transparent diagnostics, and cautious interpretation. The dynamic structure strengthens credibility when assumptions are plausible, but it also exposes violations that would remain hidden in static specifications.

title: 26  Event Studies and Dynamic Treatment Effects
text:
26.3 Identification Assumptions
The validity of event-study estimates hinges on a set of identifying assumptions that extend those underlying standard difference-in-differences designs. While the event-time framework offers greater flexibility in modeling dynamic treatment effects, it also makes these assumptions more transparent—and, in some cases, more demanding.

26.3.1 Parallel Trends in Event Time
The core identifying assumption is a form of parallel trends expressed in event time. In the absence of treatment, outcomes of treated and control units are assumed to evolve similarly at each relative time period. This assumption implies that any systematic differences observed after treatment can be attributed to the treatment itself, rather than to pre-existing or diverging trends.
Unlike static difference-in-differences, event studies allow this assumption to be partially assessed. By estimating coefficients for multiple pre-treatment periods, researchers can examine whether outcomes diverge prior to treatment. Statistically insignificant and economically small pre-treatment coefficients are often interpreted as supportive evidence for parallel trends.
However, the absence of detectable pre-trends should not be interpreted as definitive proof. Limited statistical power, noisy outcomes, or short pre-treatment windows may mask violations of the assumption.


26.3.2 No Anticipation
A closely related assumption is the absence of anticipation effects. Units are assumed not to adjust their behavior in response to knowledge of future treatment before the treatment actually occurs. If agents anticipate treatment and respond in advance, estimated pre-treatment coefficients may reflect behavioral adjustments rather than violations of parallel trends.


26.3.3 Heterogeneous Treatment Effects and Staggered Adoption
In settings with staggered treatment adoption, traditional two-way fixed effects event-study estimators impose strong restrictions on the structure of treatment effects. In particular, they implicitly assume that treatment effects are homogeneous across cohorts and over time. When this assumption fails, estimated dynamic coefficients may be difficult to interpret and may even reflect non-convex averages of underlying cohort-specific effects.
Recent work has shown that these issues can lead to misleading dynamic patterns in event-study plots, even when standard identifying assumptions appear to hold (Sun and Abraham 2021; Callaway and Sant’Anna 2021).


26.3.4 Composition of Control Groups
Event-study estimates compare treated units at a given event time to a control group consisting of units not yet treated or never treated. As event time progresses, the composition of this control group may change. Identification requires that these changes do not introduce systematic differences unrelated to treatment.
This concern is especially relevant in long panels with staggered adoption, where later-treated units serve as controls for earlier-treated units. If treatment timing is correlated with unobserved shocks, event-study estimates may be biased even in the absence of pre-treatment trends.


26.3.5 Summary
Event studies make the identifying assumptions of difference-in-differences explicit and empirically assessable. While this transparency is a major strength of the approach, it also places greater responsibility on the researcher to justify assumptions using both data and institutional context. Careful interpretation of dynamic coefficients is therefore essential, particularly in settings with heterogeneous treatment effects and staggered policy adoption.

title: 26  Event Studies and Dynamic Treatment Effects
text:
26.4 Estimation and Implementation
Having laid out the conceptual framework and identifying assumptions underlying event studies, we now turn to practical issues of estimation and implementation. While the basic idea is straightforward—regressing outcomes on a set of event-time indicators—the choice of estimator, normalization, and inference procedures plays a crucial role in the interpretation of results.

26.4.1 Baseline Event-Study Specification
\[
Y_{it} = \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \sum_{k \neq -1} \beta_k \, \mathbb{1}\{t - T_i = k\} + \\varepsilon_{it}
\]
where (T_i) denotes the period of treatment adoption for unit (i), and (k) indexes time relative to the event. One event-time indicator—typically the last pre-treatment period—is omitted as a reference category.
Each coefficient (_k) captures the average difference in outcomes between treated and control units (k) periods relative to treatment, conditional on unit and time fixed effects. The sequence of coefficients traces out the dynamic treatment response.


26.4.2 Choice of Reference Period and Normalization
The normalization of event-time coefficients is not innocuous. Omitting the final pre-treatment period is common, as it facilitates interpretation of pre-treatment coefficients as deviations from the immediate pre-treatment baseline. Alternative normalizations are possible, but they should be clearly stated and consistently applied.
Researchers should avoid overinterpreting the coefficient at event time zero. This coefficient reflects the effect during the treatment adoption period, which may be only partially exposed to treatment, depending on institutional timing.


26.4.3 Window Length and Binning
In practice, event studies often impose a finite window around the event. Very distant pre- or post-treatment periods may be sparsely populated, leading to imprecise estimates. A common approach is to bin extreme event times into a single indicator (e.g., “five or more periods after treatment”).
While binning improves precision, it also imposes restrictions on treatment dynamics. The choice of window length should balance statistical power with substantive relevance.


26.4.4 Inference and Standard Errors
As with difference-in-differences designs, inference in event studies must account for serial correlation and clustering. Standard errors are typically clustered at the unit level, reflecting the panel structure of the data.
When treatment is assigned at a higher level of aggregation—such as regions or firms—clustering should reflect the level of treatment variation. Failure to do so can result in severely understated standard errors.


26.4.5 Event Studies in the Presence of Staggered Adoption
In settings with staggered treatment adoption, conventional two-way fixed effects event-study estimators can produce misleading estimates when treatment effects are heterogeneous across cohorts or over time. Recent estimators explicitly address this issue by constructing cohort-specific comparisons and aggregating them in a transparent way.
Modern approaches, such as those proposed by Sun and Abraham (2021) and Callaway and Sant’Anna (2021), retain the intuitive appeal of event studies while avoiding the negative weighting problems inherent in traditional specifications. These methods are discussed in detail in the following chapter.


26.4.6 Interpretation and Best Practices
Event-study plots are powerful diagnostic and communication tools, but they require careful interpretation. Researchers should focus on overall patterns rather than individual coefficients, pay close attention to pre-treatment dynamics, and clearly communicate uncertainty.
Best practice involves combining event-study evidence with institutional knowledge, robustness checks, and alternative estimators. When used thoughtfully, event studies provide rich insights into the timing and evolution of causal effects.

title: 27  Synthetic Control Methods
text:
27.1 Motivation and Intuition
Many policy interventions affect a single aggregate unit (a country, a region, or a large institution) at a well-defined point in time.
In such settings, standard difference-in-differences methods are often unconvincing because there is only one treated unit and no obvious comparison group.
The synthetic control method (SCM) addresses this problem by constructing a data-driven comparison unit as a weighted average of untreated units.
The weights are chosen so that the synthetic control closely reproduces the treated unit�s pre-treatment outcomes and characteristics.
If such a combination exists before treatment, SCM assumes it provides a credible counterfactual after treatment.

title: 27  Synthetic Control Methods
text: Instead of asking which single control unit is comparable to the treated unit, SCM asks whether a combination of control units can approximate it.

title: 27  Synthetic Control Methods
text:
27.2 The Synthetic Control Framework
Consider a panel with units indexed by \(i = 1, \dots, N\) and periods \(t = 1, \dots, T\).
Unit \(i = 1\) is exposed to a treatment starting at time \(T_0\), while all other units remain untreated.
Let \(Y_{it}(0)\) denote the potential outcome without treatment, and \(Y_{it}(1)\) denote the potential outcome with treatment.
The observed outcome is:
\[
Y_{it} = D_{it} Y_{it}(1) + (1 - D_{it}) Y_{it}(0)
\]
where \(D_{it} = 1\) if unit \(i\) is treated at time \(t\), and \(D_{it} = 0\) otherwise.
The SCM estimator constructs a synthetic control as a weighted average of untreated units:
\[
\hat{Y}_{1t}(0) = \sum_{j = 2}^{N} w_j Y_{jt}
\]
where the weights satisfy:
\[
w_j \ge 0 \quad \text{and} \quad \sum_{j = 2}^{N} w_j = 1
\]
The weights are chosen to minimize the distance between the treated unit and the synthetic control in the pre-treatment period.

title: 27  Synthetic Control Methods
text:
27.3 Identification Assumptions
SCM relies on a different identifying logic than difference-in-differences.
The central assumption is that the treated unit can be approximated by a convex combination of untreated units in the absence of treatment.
If pre-treatment outcomes are well matched, SCM assumes that the same combination would continue to track the treated unit after treatment.
Formally, SCM assumes that:
\[
Y_{1t}(0) \approx \sum_{j = 2}^N w_j Y_{jt}(0), \quad \text{for } t \le T_0
\]
Unlike difference-in-differences, SCM does not rely on parallel trends. Identification is assessed visually through pre-treatment fit.

title: 27  Synthetic Control Methods
text:
27.4 Estimation and Implementation
This section describes how the synthetic control estimator is constructed in practice. While the identifying logic relies on pre-treatment fit, the actual implementation requires several modelling choices that can materially affect results.

27.4.1 Choice of Predictor Variables
The first step in implementing the synthetic control method is the selection of predictor variables. These typically include:

Pre-treatment values of the outcome variable,
Time-invariant covariates,
Aggregates or averages of pre-treatment outcomes.

The goal is to ensure that the synthetic control closely reproduces the treated unit�s characteristics and outcome dynamics prior to treatment. In practice, pre-treatment outcomes often play a dominant role, as they implicitly summarize many unobserved factors.


27.4.2 Pre-treatment Outcome Matching
Let the pre-treatment period consist of times:
\[
t = 1, \dots, T_0 - 1
\]
The quality of a synthetic control is primarily judged by how closely it tracks the treated unit during this period. A good pre-treatment fit provides evidence that the treated unit lies within the convex hull of the donor pool.
Poor pre-treatment fit signals that no weighted combination of control units can approximate the treated unit in the absence of treatment. In such cases, SCM estimates should be interpreted with caution.


27.4.3 Weight Selection and the Optimization Problem
The synthetic control weights are chosen to minimize the discrepancy between the treated unit and the weighted average of control units in the pre-treatment period.
Formally, the weights solve an optimization problem that trades off matching on covariates and matching on pre-treatment outcomes. The solution assigns larger weights to control units that more closely resemble the treated unit prior to treatment.
A key feature of SCM is that the weights are constrained to be non-negative and to sum to one. As a result, the synthetic control is a convex combination of observed units and does not extrapolate beyond the support of the data.


27.4.4 The Donor Pool
The donor pool consists of all untreated units that are eligible to contribute to the synthetic control. Its composition is crucial for credible estimation.
Including units that are fundamentally different from the treated unit can degrade pre-treatment fit. Conversely, excluding relevant control units may limit the ability to construct a good synthetic match.
In applied work, researchers often experiment with alternative donor pools as a robustness check. Transparent reporting of donor pool choices is therefore an important component of empirical SCM studies.


27.4.5 Assessing Pre-treatment Fit
Unlike regression-based methods, SCM does not rely on formal goodness-of-fit statistics. Instead, pre-treatment fit is typically assessed visually by comparing the treated unit and its synthetic control over time.
A close pre-treatment match is a necessary condition for credible post-treatment counterfactuals. When the synthetic control fails to reproduce pre-treatment trends, post-treatment differences should not be interpreted as causal effects.


27.4.6 Placebo and Falsification Tests
Because SCM typically involves a single treated unit, conventional statistical inference is not available. Instead, researchers rely on placebo and falsification tests to assess the credibility of estimated effects.
A common approach is the ‘in-space placebo test’, where the treatment is reassigned to each control unit one at a time. For each placebo unit, a synthetic control is constructed using the remaining units, and the resulting post-treatment gaps are compared to the gap observed for the treated unit.
If the treatment effect estimated for the treated unit is unusually large relative to the distribution of placebo effects, this provides evidence that the result is not driven by chance.



27.4.7 In-Time Placebo Tests
Another falsification strategy involves shifting the treatment date to a pre-treatment period. The idea is to test whether the SCM procedure detects ‘effects’ when no treatment has actually occurred.
If large post-treatment gaps appear when the placebo treatment date is set well before the true intervention, this casts doubt on the validity of the design. Credible applications typically show small and unstable gaps in these in-time placebo exercises.



27.4.8 Interpreting Magnitudes and Persistence
SCM estimates should be interpreted as ‘path-wise treatment effects’, not as average treatment effects. The magnitude, timing, and persistence of the post-treatment gap all matter for interpretation.
Short-lived or highly volatile effects may indicate anticipation, transitory shocks, or model misspecification. In contrast, persistent and stable divergences between the treated unit and its synthetic control are more consistent with sustained causal effects.



27.4.9 Sensitivity to Donor Pool and Predictors
Results from SCM can be sensitive to the choice of donor pool and the set of predictors used to construct the synthetic control.
Researchers should examine whether estimated effects remain similar when: - certain donor units are excluded, - alternative predictor sets are used, - or the pre-treatment window is modified.
Robust findings typically exhibit qualitative stability across reasonable design choices.



27.4.10 When Synthetic Control Methods Are Appropriate
SCM is most suitable in settings where: - the number of treated units is small, - the intervention occurs at a clearly defined point in time, - rich pre-treatment data are available, - and untreated units provide plausible counterfactual trajectories.
When these conditions are not met, alternative methods such as difference-in-differences or event study designs may be more appropriate.



27.4.11 Limitations and Common Pitfalls
Despite its appeal, SCM has important limitations. Poor pre-treatment fit, limited donor pools, and extrapolation beyond the support of the data can undermine credibility.
In addition, SCM does not automatically address spillovers, interference between units, or time-varying unobserved confounders. These issues must be considered carefully in empirical applications.



27.4.12 Summary
Synthetic control methods provide a transparent and intuitive framework for causal inference in comparative case studies. Their credibility hinges on pre-treatment fit, thoughtful design choices, and careful interpretation of placebo tests.
When used appropriately, SCM can yield compelling evidence in settings where traditional regression-based approaches are less convincing.
